summary: A 1971 note by two RAND authors with some thoughts on network graphics.

plainLanguage.summary: The authors like the basic idea of sending drawing instructions over the network, but want those instructions to describe more. They propose richer graphics data and a service that could translate it for simpler computers.

subtitle: RAND's comments on how network graphics should describe pictures and display capabilities.

tldr.problem: The proposal in RFC 86 focused on simple graphics commands for minimal terminals, while RAND's display hardware and applications needed richer descriptions.
tldr.mechanism: The authors suggest five broad extensions and an alternative high-level graphics format, with a network service translating it for less capable hosts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 94 offers comments and proposals for discussion. It does not define a final graphics standard.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 94 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The RFC presents discussion proposals and does not say what became of them.

sections.title: The Starting Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 94 gives initial reactions to RFC 86, a proposal intended to start discussion about network graphics. RFC 86 interprets data structures to produce graphics commands for a display, an approach the authors say had worked well before.

They want the proposal to cover both minimal terminals and more capable programs at both ends of a connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors support sending structured drawing instructions. They want the same approach to work with more kinds of computers and graphics equipment.

sections.title: Limits of Simple Display Commands
sections.content:
The authors say RFC 86's detailed limits exclude features on RAND displays, including line styles, intensity control, larger symbols, a different symbol origin, and more than seven-bit ASCII. They also note that the proposal has no way to position and open a graphics comparison window.

They recommend collecting descriptions of each host's display hardware before writing a detailed specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The simple rules leave out display features that some sites need. The authors ask network sites to describe their equipment before the rules are made more detailed.

sections.title: Extensions and Reconfiguration
sections.content:
The five suggested extensions cover the range of current and expected hardware, logical as well as pictorial data, reusable graphic definitions, separate static and changing display parts, and interpreters that can produce outputs other than one set of display commands.

For capable hosts, the authors propose a high-level macro format. A separate Data Reconfiguration Service could translate that format into the form needed by a minimal host, using stored descriptions called forms.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites could define a graphic once and send later uses by name, while updating only the parts that change. A network service could translate richer instructions for a simpler display.
